name: Anti-capitalism
summary: Anti-capitalism is the umbrella label for opposition to capitalism and its practices, whether to curb its worst effects or to replace it with another system. What it shares is the opposition itself; the sources record no common programme on ownership, markets, the state or method.

furtherReading.note: Overview of the strands and movements.

furtherReading.title: Socialism (Stanford Encyclopedia of Philosophy)
furtherReading.note: Scholarly account of the main critiques of capitalism: exploitation, domination, alienation, inefficiency.

sources.title: Anticapitalism and Culture: Radical Theory and Popular Politics
sources.author: Jeremy Gilbert (Berg, 2008)
sources.usedFor: Main defining source: chapter 3, "Another World is Possible: The Anti-Capitalist Movement" (pp. 75-106) says what the name covers, its strands, aims and figures; the book's later chapters on theory are read only for the movement.

sources.title: National Security Surveillance in Southern Africa: An Anti-Capitalist Perspective
sources.author: Jane Duncan (Bloomsbury, 2022)
sources.usedFor: Chapter 1, "National security surveillance and anti-capitalism: a theoretical discussion" (pp. 18-20): its account of anti-capitalism as a politics (no unified programme; radicals and reformers).

sources.title: Anti-capitalism: Theory and Practice
sources.author: Chris Harman (International Socialism 2:88, Autumn 2000)
sources.usedFor: A participant's account of the movement after Seattle: who its leading voices were and what they argue; a Marxist's reading, so used for who the movement names, not for its views.

sources.title: Capitalist Realism: Is There No Alternative?
sources.author: Mark Fisher (Zero Books, 2009)
sources.usedFor: A thinker's own text on anti-capitalism, which it calls for to be renewed; tied to the ideology as a key work.

sources.title: How to be an Anti-capitalist for the 21st century (essay draft 6.0; saved from the Wayback copy of the author's university page)
sources.author: Erik Olin Wright (November 2016 draft)
sources.usedFor: A sociologist's account of what anti-capitalists object to (its opening list of capitalism's harms) and of the strategies they argue over (smash, erode, tame, escape); read in full for the harms list and the strategic split.

sources.title: No Logo
sources.author: Naomi Klein (Flamingo, 2000)
sources.usedFor: Key work named by the scholarly sources as the book that popularised the anti-capitalist movement; searched by topic and read for its stated positions (chapters 14 and 17-18 and the Conclusion on regulating corporations, labour standards and unions).

sources.title: Culture Jam: How to Reverse America's Suicidal Consumer Binge - and Why We Must
sources.author: Kalle Lasn (Quill, 1999/2000)
sources.usedFor: Key work of the Adbusters founder, whom the sources count as a voice of anti-capitalist media; searched by topic and read for its stated positions (consumerism, growth, corporate power, media, left and right).

abolish-wage-labour.rationale: Duncan (ch. 1, pp. 18-19) says public ownership would free people "from having to sell their labour power", but that anti-capitalists can be radicals or reformers and "may not support the abolition of private ownership and wage labour".

central-planning.rationale: Lasn ("The New Activism", p. 119) says "Government control, central planning, public ownership" were "all shown to be fundamentally flawed" and that free markets are "far better than centralized government control of every aspect of economic life"; Albert, whom Gilbert cites (ch. 3, pp. 77-78), wants "participatory planning rather than markets or central planning".

consumerism-harmful.rationale: Lasn's book is built on the claim that consumption-driven culture is making people sick: plenitude leaves lives "shallow and meaningless" (s9, "The Ecology of Mind", p. 11) and an economy that "cannot tolerate any reduction in consumption" has a rigidity "that brings civilizations down" ("The Global Economic Pyramid Scheme", p. 95). Wright lists "profit-making, consumerism and growth that propel us towards environmental disaster" among capitalism's harms (s7).

corporate-influence.rationale: Lasn says corporations "lobby legislators and bankroll elections" and "set our industrial, economic and cultural agendas" (s9, "The Unofficial History of America™", p. 69). Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 87) sets reformers' "weak lobby" against the lobbies that can call on "great corporate institutions", and Klein (s8, ch. 14) asks what good open parliaments are if "opaque corporations were setting so much of the global political agenda in the back rooms".

future-generations.rationale: The WSF Charter (s1, ch. 3, p. 93, principle 12) centres economic and political action on "respecting nature, in the present and for future generations". Lasn calls for an economic system that works "without sacrificing the well-being of future generations" (s9, "The Global Economic Pyramid Scheme", p. 89) and says that in the expansionist model "future generations... are the dupes" (p. 94).

intersecting-oppressions.rationale: Duncan (ch. 1, p. 20) says that "Any genuine, aspirational liberation movement needs to be anti-racist, anti-capitalist and anti-imperialist", and the WSF Charter (s1, ch. 3, p. 92) speaks of capitalist globalisation's "racist, sexist and environmentally destructive dimensions".

limit-growth.rationale: In "The Global Economic Pyramid Scheme" (pp. 86-89) Lasn sides with ecological economists, who hold that the world is already "full" and that further expansion leads to an ecological nightmare, and calls the opposing view that growth can go on indefinitely "grievously irresponsible and just plain false"; on p. 95 he says the system "cannot tolerate any reduction in consumption".

local-essentials-public.rationale: Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 77) says the movement is militant in its opposition to "the privatisation of public services", and on p. 90 describes Bolivian campaigns against foreign corporate control of local water supplies that led to nationalisation of water supply.

mass-culture-pacifies.rationale: Fisher argues that a film like Wall-E exemplifies "interpassivity: the film performs our anti-capitalism for us, allowing us to continue to consume with impunity" (s6, ch. 2), and that being hooked into the entertainment matrix walls students up "against the social" (ch. 4). Lasn writes that mass media dispense "a kind of Huxleyan 'soma'" (s9, introduction) and cites a correlation between TV viewing and voter apathy ("The Ecology of Mind", p. 12).

mixed-public-service-providers.rationale: Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 77) names "the privatisation of public services" among the policies the movement militantly opposes, and on p. 88 describes ATTAC's campaigns against "the neoliberal assault on the public sphere and the public sector".

nation-first.rationale: Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 76) says the movement's commitment to democracy and egalitarianism makes it "clearly distinguishable from the other major forms of opposition to global neoliberal hegemony: nationalism and religious fundamentalism", and the WSF Charter (p. 91) commits it to "a planetary society".

nature-as-capital.rationale: Lasn faults the GDP because it "fails to assign any value to declining fish stocks or disappearing forests", endorses the ISEW and GPI that subtract such losses (s9, "The Global Economic Pyramid Scheme", pp. 88-90), and in "Redefining Progress" asks how "losses of natural capital" are "factored into the national accounts".

participatory-democracy.rationale: The WSF Charter, which Gilbert calls probably the most authoritative statement of the movement's shared values, upholds "the practices of real democracy, participatory democracy" (s1, ch. 3, p. 92), and the Zapatistas argue for "rigourously participative forms of democracy" (p. 78). Lasn likewise names "radical democracy—people telling governments and corporations what to do" (s9, "Demarketing Loops", p. 168).

production-for-use.rationale: The WSF Charter (s1, ch. 3, p. 93, principle 12) centres economic activity "on meeting the needs of people and respecting nature", and Duncan (ch. 1, p. 18) says that without private ownership people "could produce goods and services for the benefit of broader society".

public-ownership.rationale: Duncan (ch. 1, p. 18) says anti-capitalism means resources should "revert to public, collective ownership, or even no ownership at all", but Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 77) says the movement is "not committed to a singular vision of an alternative", and Lasn (p. 119) lists public ownership among ideas "shown to be fundamentally flawed".

race-social-construct.rationale: Duncan (ch. 1, p. 20) presents racial capitalism as part of anti-capitalist theory and says it "recognizes that race does not exist as a scientific fact, as all human beings are the same race and racial identities are socially constructed".

regulate-corporations.rationale: In "Grounding the Corporation" (pp. 159-162) Lasn says "We must enact tough new corporate criminal liability laws" and rewrite incorporation rules so a repeat offender's charter is revoked. Klein's Conclusion says "Political solutions — accountable to people and enforceable by their elected representatives — deserve another shot" before settling for corporate codes and monitors.

revolution-legitimate.rationale: Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 77) contrasts the revolutionary view that anti-capitalism means replacing a whole system with a reformism that may or may not seek abolition "depending on what is feasible", and Duncan (ch. 1, p. 19) cites Wright's four strategies, from smashing to taming capitalism. Wright (s7) himself argues that "system-level rupture doesn’t work as a strategy for social emancipation".

state-as-business.rationale: Fisher (ch. 3) attacks the "business ontology" in which "everything in society, including healthcare and education, should be run as a business", and Gilbert (ch. 3, p. 76) describes the neoliberal programme as one that "imposes market relations even where they are not wanted".

state-class-instrument.rationale: Duncan (ch. 1, p. 18) says anti-capitalists "are suspicious of arguments that portray the state as a politically neutral institution and instead tend to see it as an instrument for the protection of private property", whose security institutions will "most likely act to defend" the capitalist system.

total-state.rationale: The WSF Charter (s1, ch. 3, p. 92) says the Forum "is opposed to all totalitarian and reductionist views of economy, development and history and to the use of violence as a means of social control by the State".

trade-labor-env-standards.rationale: In ch. 14, "Bad Mood Rising", Klein reports that attempts to make the WTO enforce basic labour laws were dismissed and calls this one of the "failures to regulate capital" that left reform movements paralysed; her Conclusion looks to "global citizens, global rights and global responsibilities" through international law.

unions-good.rationale: Klein's Conclusion calls "the right to sit down and bargain" "the fundamental right for which the international trade union movement has struggled from its inception", something that "has always been about self-determination".

vanguard-party.rationale: Gilbert (ch. 3, pp. 78-79) says the Zapatistas, "the ideal symbol of everything that is distinctive about the anti-capitalist movement", reject "the vanguardism of the revolutionary communist tradition"; he notes only "remnants of the Leninist left" who attach themselves to the movement (p. 77).

wealth-concentration-endangers-liberty.rationale: Wright's essay lists among capitalism's familiar harms "concentrations of power and wealth that undermine democracy" (s7, opening paragraph). Lasn, in "The Unofficial History of America™" (p. 69), describes the U.S. as governed "as a corporate state" and notes that the top five hundred corporations controlled 42 percent of the world's wealth.

scope: Anti-capitalism as the umbrella name for opposition to capitalism, in the sense the sources use it: the movement that grew from the mid-1990s (the Zapatistas, Seattle 1999, the World Social Forum), whose members range from reformers who want to curb corporate power or neoliberalism to revolutionaries who want to replace the system, with no unified programme (Gilbert, ch. 3; Duncan, ch. 1; Ryley, introduction). The sources keep the name for the left-wing opposition; its Marxist, anarchist, mutualist and green strands have entries of their own, and so do the movement's neighbours such as the anti-globalization movement; this entry counts only what the sources say anti-capitalists as such hold. Critics' accounts (Mises's 'anti-capitalistic mentality') and nationalist or religious objections to capitalism are not this scope, and answer nothing.
